title: The Case of the Sneaky Sniffles
markdown:
Willow Creek School had always been a noisy place in autumn — gold leaves, crimson leaves, and children loud enough to match them. This autumn the playground had gone strangely quiet. Hallways that should have chattered were a chorus of sniffles and sighs, as if the air itself had grown tired.

Ivo the bridge tinkerer noticed it first. He was mending a loose railing on the porch, his hands as steady with a wrench as they were gentle with a fledgling. Glow, his midnight cat with emerald eyes, wove between his ankles like a shadow.

"Who is feeling so glum?" Ivo murmured, watching children shuffle past, spirits drooping. Glow offered a soft, questioning mrow.

Inside, Dr. Kellan was equally perplexed. She had come to share the wonders of the natural world and had found sleepy yawns instead of questions.

"It's most peculiar," she told Ivo, brow furrowed. "So many students, all with the same sniffles, itchy eyes, and a general sense of meh. A gray cloud over their energy."

Ivo dusted his overalls. "The air feels thick with it. My grandmother used to say even the smallest things in the dirt can make the biggest difference, for good or for ill."

That afternoon he was called to the old greenhouse to fix a drip from a pipe that snaked along the high ceiling. Inside, the air was warm and humid, thick with damp earth and decaying leaves — a different climate from the crisp autumn beyond the glass. On a sun-drenched ledge in a dusty corner sat a few forgotten apples, no longer crisp, now soft and wrinkled and covered in velvety gray-green fuzz.

Glow, who usually loved a new nook, sniffed, then backed away, fur bristling. Her purr came out low, more warning than greeting, as if she could sense a world too small for whiskers.

Dr. Kellan arrived with pockets jingling and white hair like dandelion fluff. "Ah, the greenhouse. A haven for tiny life. Let me take an air sample from this rather interesting corner." She aimed a small whirring device near the fuzzy apples.

Later, in the classroom's makeshift science corner, she peered through her portable microscope. Ivo leaned in. A faint earthy scent, like soil after rain, tickled his nose. On the screen, a universe of tiny shapes pulsed and swarmed.

"Ivo. You must see. It's teeming — far more than I expected."

Glow hopped onto the table, caution finally outvoted by curiosity. Dr. Kellan pointed.

"These are microorganisms. Living things too small to see with just our eyes. Some of what we're looking at are mold spores — tiny traveling seeds of the fungus on those apples. In a closed, damp greenhouse they fill the air. They can make eyes itch and noses drip, which would explain a school that suddenly sounds like a sniffle choir." She shifted the slide. "And here — other little lives. Some bacteria are trouble if they get where they don't belong. Some are helpers."

She indicated simpler, smoother shapes. "Those are closer to nature's janitors. They're breaking the old apple down so its goodness can go back to the earth. Fuzz is not always a villain. In the right place, it's a recycler."

Ivo tilted his head. "Grandmother again. A tiny seed can become a tree. A tiny spore can spread a cough. Or a compost."

"That's it." Dr. Kellan's face lit as the pieces sat down. "An invisible world with jobs. The mischievous ones — and the accidental travelers, like those spores — can make us feel unwell. The helpful ones work all around us, unseen, in soil and in food and even in us."

Children had gathered, lethargy forgotten, pulled by the strange image on the screen. Dr. Kellan held up a simple drawing of a spiky shape.

"Some microbes can sneak from hands to faces and cause a true infection. Washing helps there." She tapped the fuzzy-apple photograph. "But washing alone will not empty a greenhouse of spores. For that, we remove the source. Those apples have stayed too long in a warm wet room. They need to go to the compost, where their janitors are wanted, and we need the drip fixed so the air can dry."

Ivo chimed in, voice steady as a well-tuned bridge. "Soap and water for the hitchhikers on our hands. Rub like you're polishing Glow until she shines — between fingers, under nails. And no more forgotten fruit steaming on a ledge."

He mimed the wash with such enthusiasm that a boy in the front row laughed, which was the first proper laugh Ivo had heard all week. A girl copied the circles between her fingers. Glow watched, unimpressed, as if soap were a hobby for people without fur.

They did both jobs. Ivo finished the pipe so the drip stopped raining on the soil, and the greenhouse air began to smell less like a forgotten stew. Dr. Kellan bagged the apples for the compost heap beyond the playground, where decay was a career and not a classroom problem. The children washed with gusto, singing because the soap tickled, reaching every nook and the dark half-moons under their nails.

By the next afternoon the sniffles had lessened. Itchy eyes cleared. The meh moods thinned, replaced by the old hallway chatter and a playground that remembered how to shout. It was not instant magic. It was a room that had stopped feeding the wrong tiny lives into the air, and hands that had stopped helping the other kind along.

Glow inspected the empty ledge, found it boring, and sat on Ivo's foot in triumph.

"I wonder," Dr. Kellan said to the children, and to Ivo, "which of the helpers in yogurt are cousins of the janitors on that apple — and whether the soil under the oaks is as crowded as that slide. We could look. Tomorrow. After you wash."

Ivo scratched Glow's ears. He did not ask the trees to remember. He only thought, as the playground noise returned, that the smallest citizens of Willow Creek had been running the plot all along, and that a good tinkerer learned when to mend a pipe, when to move an apple, and when to use soap.
